rationale: Evidence: iteration 5 (kp 3.0, ki 0.5, kd 0.8, base 1.3, 12 mm sensors at x = -0.04..0.04, y = 0.03) is the best design so far at 384.9. The oval finishes 19 of 20 runs at about 1.97 s, so the controller is sound on gentle curves. The s-bend (progress 0.43) and slalom (progress 0.12) still fail by going off track after about one line-loss event per run, with max_error reaching the 0.06 m limit. Steering oscillation is low (0.16 on the slalom), so the robot is not jittering. It drifts out at direction changes and does not recover. Iteration 6 (kp 3.5, kd 1.0) scored lower at 348, so the extra gain did not help and I am reverting to the iteration-5 controller. Earlier changes to base_speed, sensor spacing and sensor footprint did not fix the bend failures. Iteration 2 was confounded (wider sensors plus narrower wheel_track), so the untested single levers are sensor forward position, mass and wheel_track. I am testing one lever: sensor forward position y. Each sensor moves from y = 0.03 m to y = 0.06 m, ahead of the axle, with x positions, sensor size, weights and all controller values unchanged from iteration 5. The sensors then see the line earlier, which adds lead against the lag in the steering response at direction changes. Expected result: lower max_error and fewer line-loss events on the s-bend and slalom, with the oval still finishing in about 2 s. Risk: a larger lead can make the loop less stable, which would show as higher steering_oscillation. Hypotheses to check: (a) slalom losses happen at the first sign change, where lag is largest, so more look-ahead should reduce them; (b) if steering_oscillation rises above about 0.4 with no progress gain, the loop lag is not the limit and the next test is wheel_track or mass; (c) if the oval stops finishing, the forward shift has pushed the sensors past the useful range. Next measurements: progress, line_loss_events, max_error and steering_oscillation per track, plus completion_time on the oval.
